dehydrated_text:
Not only is the monarch proclaiming a new order, but he's also asserting new values: struggle, exploitation, and toil. Before the mother gods, balance and harmony were revered—don't destroy things; worship animals as your friends, and make sacrifices if you kill them. Now this new religion advocates for destroying the world and making it yours.

The civilization practiced irrigation because controlling the earth is central to its function. After Marduk creates the world, he establishes a bureaucratic order by fashioning heaven stations for the great gods, setting constellations as patterns of the stars, appointing the year with marked-up divisions, and setting up three stars each for the 12 months.

This myth proclaims that the bureaucratic world is divinely ordained, not from priests but from the gods. The idea here is that these inventions in Sumer were meant to better govern the people. Now, Marduk builds a house as his temple and makes humans—slaves—to serve him, calling them "humans."

That's why we're invented to serve the gods before we understood that the gods served us or loved us; now we must become slaves to the gods. Beneath the celestial parts whose floor he made firm, Marduk will build a house as his luxurious abode and found a chamber for his kingship.

The gods are called the Anunnaki. Marduk takes his enemy Tingu, kills him, and creates mankind from his blood. The gods bound and inflicted the penalty on him, creating mankind to serve them while freeing the gods.

Throughout this poem, the monarch has different names: eel. What happens in these epics is they combine different traditions into one composite story. After the wise eel created mankind and imposed their service upon them, Nima performed creation with Mardok's skill.

King Marduk divided the Anunnaki gods into upper and lower groups, assigning 300 to guard the decrees of Enu and appointing them as gods. All humans are slaves, but some are better slaves than others—this explains the hierarchy.

The Epic was written to justify the existing power structure, a concept still true today. Why do we have schools? Why do we have media? Why do we have entertainment? It's all about justifying that power structure and social order.

Now, towards the end, this is establishing Babylon as the divine city where you can't leave once you're here—despite being in Babylon meaning enslavement. Let us make a shrine of great renown; your chamber will be our resting place wherein we may repose.
